claims.text: High-entropy-alloy components additively manufactured on a room-temperature substrate exhibit residual stresses.
High-entropy-alloy components additively manufactured on a room-temperature substrate exhibit dimensional deviations.
High-entropy-alloy components additively manufactured on a room-temperature substrate exhibit porosity and lack-of-fusion zones.
Preheating the build substrate reduces thermal gradients during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys.
Moderating the thermal gradient produces a more uniform solidification front.
Moderating the thermal gradient reduces residual stresses.
Moderating the thermal gradient minimizes build distortions.
Substrate preheating minimizes the thermal shock produced when molten material meets a cooler substrate.
Reduced thermal shock and cooling rate result in fewer nucleation sites for microcracks, porosity, and lack-of-fusion defects.
Controlled substrate preheating improves dimensional accuracy relative to room-temperature substrate processing.
Controlled substrate preheating increases tensile strength relative to room-temperature substrate processing.
Controlled substrate preheating increases yield stress relative to room-temperature substrate processing.
Controlled substrate preheating decreases the density of internal fabrication-induced defects relative to room-temperature substrate processing.
Preheating beyond an optimal temperature range may cause adverse microstructural changes or undesired phase transformations.
